Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Authorities investigating the case of a boy who disappeared in Kansas almost a decade ago plan to search an undisclosed residence Wednesday, the Butler County sheriff said. An age-progression photo shows what Adam Herrman would like today, as a 21-year-old man. Sheriff Craig Murphy would not disclose details about the residence or why authorities want to search it. He said his department will also search on an area of the Whitewater River, in southern Kansas, on Saturday near where Adam Herrman was last seen. Adam was 11 when he went missing in 1999. He was living in a mobile home park in Towanda, a town about 25 miles northeast of Wichita, with his adoptive parents, Doug and Valerie Herrman, authorities said. Wichita attorney Warner Eisenbise, who is representing Adam's adoptive parents, said the couple believed Adam had run away and didn't report him missing. They "really rue the fact that they didn't" report him missing, he said Monday. A few weeks ago, an undisclosed person contacted the Wichita-Sedgwick County Exploited and Missing Child Unit, expressing concern about Adam, the sheriff said. The Herrmans told Eisenbise that Adam ran away frequently, the attorney said, and they believed he was either with his biological parents or homeless. Although the Herrmans did not report him missing, "they were very worried about him," Eisenbise said. In an interview published Tuesday in The Wichita Eagle, Valerie Herrman said Adam ran away in May 1999 after she spanked him with a belt. She said she was upset but doesn't remember why, The Eagle reported. The couple never reported Adam missing, Valerie Herrman told the paper, because they feared authorities would take Adam and his siblings away because of the spanking. The couple adopted his two younger siblings as well, according to The Eagle. "We love him, and we made a terrible mistake" by not reporting him missing, Doug Herrman told The Eagle. The couple said they searched the mobile home park and other areas for two days after Adam left. "Then we came to the conclusion that the police probably have him, and they're coming to us, probably to get us in trouble," Doug Herrman told the newspaper, but the "police never came." Authorities have searched an empty lot in the Pine Ridge Mobile Home Park where the family lived. There, police found an "answer" to one of their questions, Murphy said Monday without elaborating. Eisenbise said that on December 15, authorities also searched the Herrmans' homes in Derby, outside of Wichita, and took the couple's computer, he said. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children has released an age-progression picture that depicts Adam as he might appear now: a young man with blue eyes and light-colored hair. Adam had been placed in the Herrmans' care when he was about 2, Murphy said Monday. He had been named Irvin Groeninger III when he was born June 8, 1987, Murphy said, and it was not clear when his name was changed. His biological parents relinquished their rights as parents about two decades ago, and Adam and his siblings were put in foster homes, CNN affiliate KWCH reported. "I thought what I was doing for them was in the best interest of the children, and evidently it wasn't," Irvin Groeninger, Adam's biological father,  told KWCH. "If he was still in my custody, this would have never happened." Adam's sister, Tiffany Broadfoot, 22, said she had last seen her brother about 14 years ago at a birthday party. "He had the cutest little round face, little-bitty freckles right up here on the tip of his cheek," she told the station. CNN's Taylor Gandossy contributed to this report.

# Investigators Renew Search for Adam Herrman, Missing Since 1999

**TOWANDA, Kan.** — Authorities are renewing efforts to determine what happened to Adam Herrman, a Kansas boy whose disappearance went unreported for nearly a decade, as investigators prepare additional searches and reexamine accounts provided by his adoptive family.

Adam was 11 years old when he disappeared from the Towanda-area home of his adoptive parents, Doug and Valerie Herrman, in 1999. Law-enforcement authorities did not learn that he was missing until late 2008, after one of his adoptive siblings contacted officials.

The long delay has complicated the investigation. Potential physical evidence may have been lost, witnesses’ memories have faded, and the rural areas around the family’s former home have changed over time. Even so, investigators have said they intend to continue following tips and searching locations connected to Adam’s life.

## Searches planned near former home

Authorities plan to conduct further ground searches in and around Towanda, including areas near the Herrmans’ former residence and other sites identified through interviews and tips. Depending on conditions and the information available, those efforts could involve search dogs, specialized teams and closer examinations of wooded, rural or waterside locations.

Investigators have not publicly disclosed every site under consideration, saying they do not want to compromise the inquiry. They also have cautioned that a planned search does not necessarily mean authorities have found new evidence at a particular location.

The central unanswered question remains whether Adam ran away, as his adoptive parents have said, or whether he died or was harmed before his disappearance became known.

No one has been charged in connection with Adam’s disappearance.

## Adoptive parents say Adam ran away

Doug and Valerie Herrman have said Adam left their home after he was disciplined and never returned. They have acknowledged that they did not report him missing.

According to their account, they believed Adam might have gone back to members of his biological family or otherwise left voluntarily. They also have said they feared that notifying authorities could result in the removal of other children from their home because the family had previously come under scrutiny over allegations involving discipline and abuse.

The Herrmans later told some relatives that Adam was no longer living with them, reportedly allowing others to believe he had returned to state custody. That claim became a major focus of the investigation because state officials had no record showing that Adam had been returned to foster care or placed elsewhere.

Through their attorney, the Herrmans have maintained that they did not kill Adam and do not know where he is. Their lawyer has said the couple have cooperated with investigators and want Adam found. The attorney has also urged the public not to treat suspicion as proof, emphasizing that the failure to report Adam missing, while deeply troubling, does not by itself establish what happened to him.

Investigators, however, have continued to scrutinize the couple’s explanation, including the circumstances surrounding Adam’s last known days at the home and the reasons no missing-person report was filed.

## A disappearance hidden for years

Adam’s case drew national attention because he effectively vanished from official view.

After being placed in foster care, Adam and two of his younger siblings lived with the Herrmans and were later adopted by them. Relatives said they were given varying explanations for why Adam was no longer present. For years, there was no broad public search, no missing-child bulletin and no immediate law-enforcement response because authorities had not been told he was gone.

The case finally came to light when a family member raised concerns in 2008. Investigators then began reconstructing events dating back to 1999, interviewing relatives, former neighbors, school officials and others who had known Adam.

Authorities also examined records to determine whether Adam had appeared in another school district, received government services or had any documented contact under his own or another name. No confirmed trace of him after his disappearance has been publicly announced.

## Biological relatives seek answers

Members of Adam’s biological family have said they were devastated to learn that he had been missing for years. They have disputed the suggestion that he simply returned to them, saying they did not have Adam and were not told at the time that he had disappeared.

His biological relatives have expressed both hope and fear: hope that Adam somehow survived and may still be found, and fear that the failure to report him missing means something more serious happened.

Family members have said they want a complete accounting of Adam’s final days in the Herrman home. They have also voiced frustration that they lost years in which they might have searched for him, circulated his photograph or appealed publicly for information.

For them, the renewed searches are about both evidence and closure. Even if investigators cannot find Adam alive, relatives have said they want to know where he is and what happened to him.

## Investigators ask public for information

Authorities continue to ask anyone who had contact with the Herrman family in the late 1990s — particularly anyone who saw Adam, visited the family’s home or heard contemporaneous statements about his absence — to contact investigators.

They are especially interested in information that can help establish Adam’s last confirmed sighting and test the various explanations given for his disappearance.

Officials have stressed that seemingly minor memories could be important. Because Adam was not reported missing when he vanished, investigators must now rebuild a timeline from old records and recollections rather than from evidence collected immediately after the event.

The renewed investigation underscores the unusual difficulty of the case: authorities are searching not only for a missing child, but also for the truth about nearly a decade in which almost no one outside the household knew he was gone.
